title: Lamar Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Lamar wells have a 41-foot median depth, with typical completed well costs of $7,400-$14,300.
h1: Lamar, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost
intro_html:
If you are buying land or a home near Lamar, the local well records point to unusually shallow wells in much of the area. The median reported depth is 41 feet, and 74% of wells are under 100 feet. That does not guarantee the same result on a particular parcel. Well construction, water quality, pumping equipment, and the permit’s allowed use still need separate review.

This data covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Lamar in Prowers County. It includes 889 wells in Colorado Division of Water Resources records, but only 490 are recorded as constructed. Neighboring areas such as Wiley, McClave, and Granada can provide useful context, but the well on the property you are considering matters most.

sections.heading: Lamar well depths reflect shallow plains geology
sections.html:
Lamar’s recorded wells have a 41-foot median total depth. The middle half runs from 25 to 105 feet, so a driller bidding a typical residential well here may be looking at a relatively short hole compared with many mountain or fractured-granite locations. Still, the range is wide: the 90th-percentile depth is 356 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 3,900 feet.

The depth mix explains why averages can mislead. Seventy-four percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 12% fall from 100 to 300 feet and another 12% from 300 to 600 feet. A parcel can differ because of local alluvium, sedimentary layers, target aquifer, permitted use, or the need to improve water quality or reliability.

sections.heading: What Lamar wells produce at the pump
sections.html:
Among the 71 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 150.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-six percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 23% are in the 5-to-15 range. Only 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, and none fall in the 1-to-5 range.

Those figures are encouraging for this plains setting, but a yield record is not a guarantee for a new hole. Ask for the original well test and confirm whether the reported rate is a short test result or a sustainable pumping rate. A domestic exempt well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute, and the permit’s use controls what the water can legally serve.

sections.heading: Lamar water levels are shallow, with a slight recorded change
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are shallow. The median depth to water is 8 feet, with the middle half from 8 to 9 feet. That can simplify pumping, but it also means groundwater is close to surface conditions. Proper casing and grout, a sanitary seal, and a wellhead protected from surface drainage are important.

The decade series shows a small change rather than a dramatic documented decline: the median was 8 feet below surface in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s. Only 41 wells report a static water level, so do not treat the series as a complete basin trend. Measure the well on the property and review nearby records before relying on it for a home or irrigation plan.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use around Lamar
sections.html:
Lamar has a long permit history, with records beginning in the 1950s and the newest permit issued in 2023. The largest decade was the 1990s, with 141 permits, followed by 103 in the 2000s. There were 49 permits in the 2020s, so nearby activity has continued rather than ending with older agricultural development.

The records include domestic or household wells at 34%, irrigation at 21%, monitoring at 20%, and stock use at 10%. Most named aquifers are unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 800 wells; 24 identify the Dakota and 14 identify the Alluvial aquifer. No Denver Basin aquifer wells appear in this local set.

The most frequently listed drillers are Hoffman, including Hoffman, Earl, with 113 records; Authorized, including Pe and Pg, with 97; and Ark Valley Pump & Supply, including Smith Jr., William, with 28. These are record names, not a recommendation or a current availability check.

sections.heading: A Lamar well budget starts with the hole, not the whole system
sections.html:
For Lamar’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 41-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $1,400 to $2,300. That is only the drilling portion. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,400 to $14,300.

A bid should state what is included: permit work, casing and grout, drilling through difficult layers, development and testing, pump sizing, controls, trench length, electrical service, and restoration. The shallow median keeps some Lamar projects affordable, but an unusually deep hole or a more demanding site can move the price well beyond the local median example.

sections.heading: Check Lamar contamination, setbacks, and building constraints
sections.html:
Water quantity is not the only risk. Within about 10 miles of Lamar, the mapped environmental records include 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped sites do not prove a specific parcel is contaminated, but they are a reason to review the property’s location, prior uses, and available water-quality results.

Low-yield wells and dry holes are uncommon in the reported yield records, but the sample is limited because only 71 wells report a pump yield. Before closing, obtain the well permit, construction report, pump test, static water level, and recent laboratory testing. Confirm septic setbacks from the well and property lines, room for a replacement system, driveway access for a rig, and whether the planned home and water use fit the permit.

sections.heading: What to do before buying or building near Lamar
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a countywide assumption. Compare nearby permitted wells in Lamar and, where useful, records from Wiley, McClave, and Granada. Pay attention to depth, aquifer name, reported yield, water level, well age, and permitted use. A neighboring well can improve your estimate, but it cannot substitute for a site-specific investigation.

For a purchase, make well and septic records part of due diligence and use inspection or testing deadlines that allow time to investigate. For a new build, have a Colorado water professional confirm the permit path before choosing the house location, septic area, driveway, and utility route. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Keep the driller’s scope and the pump, trenching, and electrical allowances separate in the construction budget.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Lamar, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Lamar is 41 feet. The middle half runs from 25 to 105 feet, and 74% of wells are under 100 feet. Depth still varies substantially: the 90th percentile is 356 feet, and the deepest record is 3,900 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Lamar?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At Lamar’s 41-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,400 to $2,300. A completed system including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,400 to $14,300.

faq.q: How much water do Lamar wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 71 Lamar-area wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 15.0 to 150.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-six percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. These records are useful guidance, not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Lamar, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. There are 13 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with 1 historic mine feature and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the property’s well through a qualified laboratory and review nearby environmental history before relying on it.

faq.q: Are Lamar well water levels dropping?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 8 feet below surface in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s. That suggests a small recorded change, not proof of a major decline. Only 41 wells report static water levels, so check the subject well and nearby records rather than relying on the decade figures alone.
